papers.title: Development of the Biopen: a handheld device for surgical printing of adipose stem cells at a chondral wound site
papers.abstract: We present a new approach which aims to translate freeform biofabrication into the surgical field, while staying true to the practical constraints of the operating theatre. Herein we describe the development of a handheld biofabrication tool, dubbed the 'biopen', which enables the deposition of living cells and biomaterials in a manual, direct-write fashion. A gelatin-methacrylamide/hyaluronic acid-methacrylate (GelMa/HAMa) hydrogel was printed and UV crosslinked during the deposition process to generate surgically sculpted 3D structures. Custom titanium nozzles were fabricated to allow printing of multiple ink formulations in a collinear (side-by-side) geometry. Independently applied extrusion pressure for both chambers allows for geometric control of the printed structure and for the creation of compositional gradients. In vitro experiments demonstrated that human adipose stem cells maintain high viability (>97%) one week after biopen printing in GelMa/HAMa hydrogels. The biopen described in this study paves the way for the use of 3D bioprinting during the surgical process. The ability to directly control the deposition of regenerative scaffolds with or without the presence of live cells during the surgical process presents an exciting advance not only in the fields of cartilage and bone regeneration but also in other fields where tissue regeneration and replacement are critical.

summary_en.motivation: To translate freeform biofabrication into the surgical setting with a handheld device.

summary_en.motivation: To evaluate whether mild peri-operative hypothermia affects the hemostatic efficacy of tranexamic acid in total hip arthroplasty.
summary_en.method: Retrospective clinical study comparing blood loss and transfusion rates between hypothermic and normothermic patients.
summary_en.result: Hypothermia may reduce the effectiveness of tranexamic acid, leading to increased transfusion requirements.
summary_en.validation: Statistical analysis of clinical patient data.

papers.title: Subspine Impingement: 2 Case Reports of a Previously Unreported Cause of Instability in Total HIP Arthroplasty
papers.abstract: Background Instability is a common cause of revision hip arthroplasty and is frequently due to improper component placement and subsequent component impingement. Impingement of the greater trochanter upon the anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) has been described as a cause of symptomatic femoroacetabular impingement (FAI), but has never been described as a cause of instability following total hip arthroplasty (THA). Case review We present 2 cases of patients undergoing THA. Each patient was evaluated preoperatively and found to have a prominent AIIS, which was concerning due to it overhanging the anterolateral acetabular lip. Both patients had intraoperative posterior instability of their THA, the cause of which was determined to be impingement of the greater trochanter upon a prominent AIIS. Open resection of the AIIS was performed with subsequent resolution of impingement. Literature review AIIS impingement has been reported as a cause of symptomatic FAI. In these case reports, open or arthroscopic resection of the AIIS resulted in resolution of symptoms. Morphologically distinct subtypes of the AIIS have been previously described based upon computed tomography, and some subtypes are associated with a high risk of impingement in the native hip. No previous studies have described this phenomenon in the setting of THA. Clinical relevance Instability is a common cause of revision THA. Impingement of the greater trochanter upon a prominent AIIS is a previously unreported cause of THA instability which can be addressed with intraoperative resection of the AIIS with good result.

summary_zh.motivation: 报道THA术后一种新的不稳原因：髂前下棘撞击。
summary_zh.method: 两例THA患者术中发现大转子与突出AIIS撞击导致后向不稳。
summary_zh.result: 切除AIIS后撞击消失，稳性恢复。
summary_zh.validation: 临床案例报告及文献回顾。

summary_en.motivation: To report a previously unrecognized cause of instability in total hip arthroplasty due to subspine impingement.
summary_en.method: Two case studies of patients undergoing THA with intraoperative posterior instability attributed to greater trochanter impingement on a prominent AIIS, treated by open AIIS resection.
summary_en.result: Resection of the AIIS resolved impingement and instability in both cases.
summary_en.validation: Clinical case report with literature review.
